newsitem.title: CHINA: Hutchison seen spending on core areas.
newsitem.headline: Hutchison seen spending on core areas.

text.p: Hutchison Whampoa Ltd Ltd caused a stir in the bond market this week with a US$2 billion debt issue, but the company is unlikely to pursue an aggressive acquisition binge and instead focus on existing businesses, analysts said.

"I don't necessarily believe that there's any specific thing they've got up their sleeve," said Standard Chartered analyst Mark Coggins, largely dismissing speculation that the company would hit the acquisition trail after completing the largest-ever global issue of Yankee bonds by a non-U.S. company.
"You can easily see how they can use that money without doing anything dramatic," he said.
Hutchison has invested heavily in recent years in its telecommunications, container terminal and manufacturing businesses, and analysts said it will continue to do so.
Meanwhile, the group's property arm would require further heavy investment as numerous projects come on line in the next few years, analysts said.
Nam Park at ING Barings said he expected Hutchison to put in excess of HK$20 billion into capital spending and investment in 1997 and to continue in this vein for the next several years.
The company spent HK$11 billion in 1996.

"I think the management would like to redress the balance towards generating more stable, more predictable profits," Park said, pointing to the heavy reliance on property development profits and exceptional-item contributions in recent years.

Other analysts agreed that Hutchison's stepped up capital spending program would lay the groundwork for increased earnings in the future. "They are now coming back into a new growth phase," said Schroders Securities analyst Mark Simpson.
Simpson pointed to earnings feeding through from what he termed "phase one" investments like Hutchison's British telecommunications unit Orange Plc.
"Now they are looking to fund phase two, which in my mind is a continuation or widening of existing business," he said.
Although analysts were highly sceptical that the company would seek large-scale acquisitions, they would not rule out smaller purchases that fit well with Hutchison's core areas.

But pinning down just where an acquisition might make sense for the company was difficult, they said. Some said that a substantial presence in Hong Kong and licensing issues in other markets made telecom acquisitions highly unlikely.
But the company could look at port-related purchases as it pushes global expansion in this area, said one analyst.
Any sort of non-core purchase, however, would not make sense given Hutchison's history of organic growth and investment in its staple businesses, analysts said.
"The program that they have pursued in recent years seems to be very much on board," said Simpson. "I don't see what additional leg to the business they would want to add."
The success of the debt offering, which was increased from an original US$1 billion, could also be viewed as having implications beyond Hutchison itself, analysts said.
The market's strong acceptance was seen as a show of continued faith in Hong Kong following its July 1 handover to China after 156 years of British rule.
In addition, it could mark the start of a greater number of Hong Kong companies turning to debt rather than equity markets as they traditionally have done to fuel their development, analysts said.
"It was always going to be someone like Hutchison that would lead the way," said Coggins.

"There is no doubt that the top ranking Hong Kong blue chip companies will be able to tap world debt markets. The companies that are able to do so will have much more durability than those who have to keep going to the equity market."
